A hook that fails closed is meant to block any send that is not addressed to the asker alone; that block has to be proven with test sends before go-live.
edits.example: Jordan texts: 'Email me the camp comparison.' The full comparison arrives in her own inbox as plain text from the family sender address. A send with anyone else on the To, cc or bcc line, or one sent as a reply-all, is meant to be blocked by the hook, and that block is tested before go-live.
edits.how:
A send-only mail tool on a dedicated family sender account: the gog MCP server with the write flag plus its separate `--allow-gmail-send` flag and only `gmail_send_message` allowed, granted to `

-main` only. A `before_tool_call` hook blocks the call unless the recipient equals the owner address of the calling agent and cc and bcc are empty; it also blocks any call that carries reply context or a reply-all target (upstream says a send needs 'recipients or a reply-all target', so a reply-all could reach other people with no recipient field at all), a send-as alias, or an HTML body (`body_html`), so mail goes out as plain text. A block is terminal and the hook fails closed. Do not rely on rewriting the recipient: the docs describe rewrites for host-owned tool parameters only. An in-house daily send cap. Sign the sender account in with a send-only grant if the installed gog supports it (the upstream command reference lists a `send` mode for `--gmail-scope` on `gog auth add`), so that the token cannot read that mailbox.
caveats: The promise that nobody else can be a recipient rests on an in-house hook, and it is not yet shown that the hook sees every field that can set a recipient: to, cc and bcc, and also the reply fields, because the upstream page for the mail tool says a send needs 'recipients or a reply-all target', so a reply-all could address other people with no recipient listed. A seeded send to a non-owner address and a seeded reply-all must both be blocked before this goes live.
The hook blocks a wrong recipient; it does not correct it, because the docs describe rewriting parameters for host-owned tools only.

Pinning the recipient does not close every way out. The mailed text is often built from research results, and a link in it, or a remote image in an HTML mail, can carry private text in its address to whoever runs that site once the link is clicked or the mail is opened (the 'lethal trifecta' post the roadmap takes its rule from names loading an image and offering a link to click as ways data gets out). The upstream tool accepts an HTML body, so the hook refuses it and the first version sends plain text only; a link in the text is still only as trustworthy as the result it came from.
Plain text means a table arrives as lined-up text, not as a formatted table; an HTML body is a later choice and would need the hook to refuse remote images.
It needs a dedicated family sender Google account with a send grant, set up by hand outside OpenClaw, and a daily send cap that is in-house code (no built-in cap was found).
gog's quickstart says a Google sign-in app left in Testing issues tokens that expire after seven days, so the sender account needs the app published to In production, as the mail reader (G015) does.
unverified: That the hook sees every field of the gog MCP send tool that can set a recipient: the upstream MCP page names recipients, reply context, a reply-all target and send-as aliases as inputs but does not list the tool's input schema, so whether cc and bcc are separate fields is not known. Read the schema from the installed server and prove the block with a seeded send to a non-owner address and a seeded reply-all.
A daily send cap is in-house code; no built-in cap was found in the pages read.
Creating the dedicated family sender account and granting its send scope is a manual step outside OpenClaw.

That `gog auth add --gmail-scope send` exists on the installed version and that the MCP send tool works under a send-only grant: the flag was read in the upstream command reference, and gog is not installed on this Mac.
edits.safety: The send tool sits on each parent's own agent, which holds private data, so the recipient pin is the protection: a fail-closed hook blocks any send that is not addressed to the calling agent's owner alone, with no cc or bcc, no reply or reply-all target and no send-as alias, and the tool is granted to no shared or mail-reading agent. Mail leaves from a dedicated family sender address, not from a parent's own account, and as plain text, so it cannot carry a remote image that reports back when the mail is opened; a link in the text can still do that if it is clicked.
